nameStory: The unicorn clubtail gets its magical name from the distinctive horn-like projection on the male's face, which resembles a unicorn's horn when viewed head-on. Like all clubtails, it also has the characteristic swollen 'club' at the tip of its abdomen, making it look like it's carrying a tiny baseball bat.
description: The unicorn clubtail is a medium-sized dragonfly with the classic clubtail build - a sturdy body ending in that telltale swollen tip. Adults typically measure about 2-2.5 inches long with clear wings that shimmer in sunlight. Their bodies are primarily brown and yellow with intricate patterns, and they have prominent, widely-separated eyes that give them excellent vision for hunting. Like all dragonflies, they're fierce aerial predators that snatch mosquitoes, flies, and other small insects right out of the air.

idTips.label: Horn-like projection
idTips.description: Males have a distinctive pointed projection on the front of their face that's visible when looking head-on - this is the 'unicorn horn' that gives them their name

idTips.label: Clubbed abdomen
idTips.description: The tip of the abdomen is noticeably swollen and club-shaped, wider than the rest of the body segment

idTips.label: Separated eyes
idTips.description: Unlike many dragonflies, the large compound eyes don't touch at the top of the head but are clearly separated

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often seen perched on bare ground, rocks, or low vegetation near water rather than hovering constantly like some dragonflies

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are mostly transparent with subtle brownish veining and may show a faint amber tinge at the base

habitat: Unicorn clubtails prefer slow-moving or still waters like ponds, lakes, and sluggish streams with muddy or sandy bottoms. You'll often spot them near the edges of these water bodies, especially where there are open areas of bare soil or rocks for perching. They favor waters with emergent vegetation like cattails and pickerelweed, but avoid heavily shaded forest pools.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with peak emergence in early June. Look for freshly emerged individuals with soft, pale coloration resting near water.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August. Adults are most active on warm, sunny days, hunting and mating. Males establish territories along shorelines.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases in September, with the last adults typically seen in early October. Late-season individuals may appear more worn with tattered wing edges.
seasonality.winter: Adults are completely absent. Nymphs (aquatic juveniles) overwinter buried in mud at the bottom of ponds and streams, taking 2-3 years to mature.

funFact: Unicorn clubtail nymphs are the ultimate hide-and-seek champions - they bury themselves completely in mud or sand at the bottom of ponds with only their eyes and the tip of their abdomen (which acts like a snorkel) poking out, sometimes staying motionless for hours waiting for prey to walk right over them!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the lilypad clubtail, which shares similar size and habitat. The key difference is that male unicorn clubtails have that distinctive facial horn while lilypad clubtails don't. Memory trick: 'Unicorn = horn' - if you see the facial projection on a male, you've found your unicorn!
compareHints: The unicorn clubtail differs from its close relative, the lilypad clubtail, primarily in the male's facial features - unicorn clubtails have that distinctive horn-like projection while lilypad clubtails have a more rounded face. Unicorn clubtails also tend to prefer more open water areas, while lilypad clubtails are more often found around vegetation-rich pond edges. Both species have the characteristic clubbed abdomen and separated eyes that distinguish them from other dragonfly families.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Unicorn Clubtail, the Lilypad Clubtail lacks the distinctive horn-like facial projection and tends to perch more often on floating vegetation rather than shoreline perches.
